How is New Jersey organized when you sell a house here?

New Jersey has 21 counties. Beneath them sit 566 municipalities, the count the state Division of Local Government Services uses when it says each municipality with delinquent taxes must hold a tax sale every year.

A home sale touches both levels, so it helps to know who does what.

  • The municipal tax collector and tax assessor handle your bill and your assessed value.
  • The county clerk records deeds and mortgages.
  • The County Board of Taxation hears assessment appeals.
  • The county sheriff runs foreclosure auctions.
  • The county Surrogate's Court handles probate when an owner has died.

We keep guides for several counties, including Bergen, Monmouth, Ocean County Clerk and Hunterdon County Clerk. The county lists further down this page link to every city and county guide we have.

What happens if property tax goes unpaid in New Jersey?

Property tax is a continuous lien on the real estate, and it is due in four installments on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Delinquent amounts can accrue interest of up to 8 percent on the first $1,500 and up to 18 percent above that, and a year-end penalty of up to 6 percent can apply past $10,000.

If the balance stays open, the municipality can sell a tax sale certificate. That sells a lien, not the title, and the certificate should be recorded with the county clerk within 90 days. An owner who redeems before foreclosure pays a penalty of 2, 4 or 6 percent plus interest. A lien holder can start a Superior Court foreclosure after two years.

Selling earlier leaves more room. Read more on tax sales, tax liens and property tax appeals.

If the assessment looks too high, the state's appeal page sets these rules:

  • File with the County Board of Taxation, or go straight to the Tax Court if the assessment is over $1,000,000.
  • The deadline is April 1, or May 1 after a municipal revaluation.
  • Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties use a January 15 deadline instead.
  • After a county board judgment, you have 45 days to go to the Tax Court.

How does foreclosure work in New Jersey, and can I still sell?

New Jersey is a judicial foreclosure state, so the lender has to go through the court.

The timeline on the NJ Courts self-help page runs like this:

  • The lender first sends a Notice of Intent to Foreclose. You have 30 days from receipt to pay off the loan, make other arrangements or ask for mediation.
  • If a complaint follows, you have 35 days to file an answer. With no answer the case is uncontested and stays with the Office of Foreclosure.
  • Before a default is entered, the lender must give a final chance to cure 14 days ahead. You then have 10 days to respond and 45 days to cure or make other arrangements.
  • After final judgment and a writ of execution, the sheriff has 150 days to hold the auction. Each side can request two stays.
  • Once the sale happens, you have 10 days to redeem. Surplus beyond the debt comes back to you, and a shortfall can be pursued by the lender.

The Notice of Intent must tell you that you can sell or transfer the title, so a sale before the auction stays possible. The courts also warn about foreclosure rescue scams and point to free HUD or NJHMFA certified counselors. See our sheriff sale guide.

What does a seller pay at closing in New Jersey?

The seller pays the Realty Transfer Fee, set by the price in the deed. For a total of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000, $3.35 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 from $200,000 to $350,000. Higher prices use a second schedule, and qualifying residential sales over $1,000,000 add a graduated fee that starts at 1 percent.

Exempt deeds include transfers between spouses, between parent and child and estate distributions by an executor or administrator. Seniors, blind or disabled sellers and low and moderate income housing get lower rates on Form RTF-1. Sales tax is not due on a home sale.

Do I owe income tax when I sell a New Jersey house?

New Jersey calculates gain the way the federal return does. The principal residence exclusion covers up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for joint filers, if you owned and lived in the home for two of the last five years.

Every owner files a GIT/REP form. Residents who stay in New Jersey usually file GIT/REP-3 to avoid an estimated payment. Nonresidents generally owe an estimate of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the net gain, paid before or at closing, unless an exemption applies. Our capital gains guide covers the filing side.

The state's seller guide adds that a homestead benefit credit has to be taken at closing if you moved, or it goes toward the new owners' taxes. Current relief programs are ANCHOR, Stay NJ and Senior Freeze, all subject to the state budget. See our homestead guide.

What should heirs know before selling an inherited house in New Jersey?

Start with the Surrogate's Court in the county where the owner lived. The Morris County Surrogate explains that when there is a will, probate proves it is authentic and makes it part of the county record. When there is no will, the estate goes through administration, and the court can require a surety bond based on the estate's value. Probate or administration cannot be completed until 10 days after the date of death.

Filing methods and fees vary by county. Morris County takes filings online, by mail or by appointment, with starting fees of $100 for probate and $125 for administration.

Transfer fee exemptions cover estate distributions by an executor or administrator. A sale to an outside buyer is a different kind of transaction, so confirm with an estate attorney how it will be treated. Our probate guide and inheritance tax guide cover the rest.

What if the house has tenants?

In New Jersey a landlord cannot evict without going to court. Only a Special Civil Part officer can carry out an eviction, and a lockout by anyone else is illegal. After a judgment for possession, the landlord may apply for a warrant of removal, which cannot be issued until three business days after the judgment. A residential tenant then gets at least three business days after the warrant is served.

The landlord has 30 days from judgment to apply for the warrant, and the officer has 30 days from issuance to act, unless a court order or written agreement pauses the clock. A buyer of an occupied house inherits that process, so the lease matters. Read the eviction process, eviction notices and landlord and tenant law.

Which property problems come up most in New Jersey sales?

Flood risk has its own rule. Since March 20, 2024, sellers must disclose on the property condition disclosure statement whether the home is in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area or Moderate Flood Hazard Area, plus any actual knowledge of flooding, before the buyer is obligated. NJDEP points sellers to its Flood Notification Report Tool.

  • Lead paint: for homes built before 1978, sellers disclose known lead-based paint and hazards on the federal form.
  • Radon: the state recommends fixing levels of 4 picocuries per liter or more in the lowest livable level. A buyer's test has to be done by a DEP certified tester.
  • Wells and septic: testing and septic certification may be required before closing.

Our seller disclosure guide explains what to expect on the forms.

What does an as-is cash sale look like in New Jersey?

An as-is cash sale means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and does not ask you to repair it first. The paperwork still follows New Jersey practice. Most closings happen in person at an attorney, agent or title company office. When a licensee prepares the contract, it must include an attorney review clause giving both sides three business days to consult a lawyer.

The title agent or the buyer's attorney usually records the deed afterward. Cash removes the lender from the table. It does not remove disclosure duties, tax forms or the transfer fee.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties are in New Jersey?

There are 21 counties. Each one has its own clerk, sheriff, Surrogate and Board of Taxation, so call the county where the house sits.

Is New Jersey a judicial foreclosure state?

Yes. The lender must go through the court, starting with a Notice of Intent to Foreclose that gives you 30 days to respond.

Can I sell during foreclosure?

Yes. The Notice of Intent must tell you that you can sell or transfer the title. After a sheriff's sale you have 10 days to redeem, so selling earlier gives you more room.

Who pays the Realty Transfer Fee?

The seller pays it when the deed is recorded. Exemptions exist, such as transfers between spouses or parent and child.

When is the property tax appeal deadline?

Usually April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties use January 15.

Do I need a probate case before selling an inherited house?

The county Surrogate's Court handles probate or administration, and neither can be completed until 10 days after the date of death. Call the Surrogate in the county where the owner lived to confirm the steps.

Do I have to fix the house before a cash sale?

No repairs are required for an as-is sale, but New Jersey flood, lead paint and other disclosure rules still apply.
